memory_candidates.content: scripts/check-module-invariants.sh derives REPO_ROOT from its own BASH_SOURCE path (`REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"; cd "$REPO_ROOT"`) and cd's there unconditionally. A modified scratch copy of this script placed outside scripts/ (e.g. in a /tmp scratchpad) silently cd's to the WRONG directory and walks a near-empty or unrelated tree instead of erroring -- producing misleading PASS/FAIL results rather than a crash. Any scratch-testing of a change to this script (e.g. a narrowness/regression check via a throwaway synthetic decls2 row) must place the copy inside scripts/ itself (a dot-prefixed throwaway filename works, e.g. scripts/.narrowness-test.sh) so REPO_ROOT still resolves correctly, then delete it afterward.

When a lint/gate scanner needs to exempt a measured set of findings without silently absorbing future unmeasured ones, prefer a tuple-keyed exemption set over a bare-name/single-key exemption set. A bare-name exemption (e.g. a set of strings) permanently disables that whole name's bucket, so a genuinely new future collision on the same name is never reported again. A composite-key exemption (e.g. (base, outer_namespace, inner_namespace)) records exactly what was measured; a new, unmeasured occurrence sharing only the base name is still caught. This trade-off (more entries and slightly more scanner logic, in exchange for narrowness) is worth it whenever the exemption is meant to be a permanent, reviewed record rather than a temporary suppression.
